utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters; good morning to the OTP and Defence counsel; good morning, General Krstic. Good morning, Professor Radinovic. We are going to proceed with your testimony. You will be continuing under oath, let me remind you. And Mr. Visnjic has the floor. Your witness, Mr. Visnjic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I should like to ask the usher to give the witness Prosecution Exhibit 609. We'll start off with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, you have before you a daily combat report -- no. I apologise. It is the interim combat report of the command of the Zvornik Brigade. It is dated the 15th of July, 1995. Could you please take a look at the second part of this report - I think it is the second part - which speaks about prisoners of war. Could you focus on that section and tell the Trial Chamber how you understood this document with respect to the role of the Zvornik Brigade, or rather its commander, in the events on the territory of the Zvornik Brigade and in connection with the prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an interim combat report, as it says, of the command of the Zvornik Brigade to the command of the Drina Corps. It is the report on the day when the commander of the brigade, at the request of the commander of the Drina Corps, that the Zvornik Brigade return from Zepa because there was a great crisis underfoot in the zone -- in his zone of responsibility. So that is the time when the brigade commander, with his units engaged in Zepa, returned to his zone of responsibility. And he is reporting, informing the commander of the Drina Corps about the situation in his zone of responsibility. In the first part of the report he speaks about the situation in general, the enemy forces that have been engaged, and we see that there are about 3.000 armed members of the 28th Division. And it also speaks about a strong attack, in-depth attack in the depth of the Zvornik Brigade, coming from the Tuzla axis. He mentions the artillery, high-calibre weapons, tanks, and so on. And at the positions of the 4th and 6th Battalions, they are battalions on the forefront of the defence line where the zone of defence was. And it also talks about the measures undertaken. A direct response to your question is the following: On the second page of this report, it says, and I quote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Professor. I apologise for interrupting, but to answer directly to the question, you should focus on giving us direct answers to the question. Because we are acquainted with this document, so there's no need for you to repeat everything that has already been said. So please try to give us a direct answer to the question put to you by Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Visnjic, would you try to guide your witness to giving us direct answers to the heart of the matter. Thank you. I apologise for interrupting at that point.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I too apologise. I thought it would be interesting to see the figure of the armed men in area of the Zvornik Brigade and the intensity of the 2nd Corps on the zone of responsibility. I thought that that is relevant for this trial. But if that is common knowledge already, then I apologise. Anyway, he says in the report that an additional -- there is an additional burden for us in the -- and the -- is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout schools in the brigade area, as well as obligations of security and restoration of the terrain. "This command cannot take care of these problems any longer as it has neither the material nor other resources. If no one takes on this responsibility, I will be forced to let them go." In this part of the report, we see several facts which are extremely important, vital for this trial. The commander of the Zvornik Brigade knows, therefore, that in his zone of responsibility there are prisoners of war. That is the first fact that we see from this report. The second fact is that he says that this is using up the brigade's resources, which he is lacking in, anyway, for the defence, for the defence of his zone of responsibility, and he mentions the expenditure of resources in order to secure the prisoners and with the sense of clearing up the terrain, so those are the obligations. And he says that he cannot take on this burden, this additional burden any longer and take care about those problems. For me, the report means that he is well aware of the fact that the prisoners are in his area of responsibility, that up until that time he has provided security for them, that his men are doing that, but that they can no longer be responsible for that; so that this leads us to conclude that the commander does know about the prisoners, but that quite certainly the commander does not know that already at that time, according to the data and information that I learnt about by reading the documents for this testimony of mine, that already at that time the prisoners had already been liquidated in his zone of responsibility. So it is quite certain that he does not know about that because, had he known about it, he would have known that he was responsible for that, and that fact would not have been disclosed; it would have been hidden because, in this way, he steps into the chain of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to hand Exhibit 675, Prosecution Exhibit 675, to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, could you please turn to page 3 of this document in the Serbian version, point 4, the part which relates to the situation in the territory. And in the context of the previous question I asked you, could you give us your comments on this document and this part of the report, in fact.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is point 4 on page 3, the situation in the territory. These facts and the appeal launched by the commander of the brigade to his superiors I understand in the same context and in the same sense that I spoke about in answer to the first document, when commenting on the first document. The commander of the brigade says that it is incomprehensible, "It is inconceivable to me that somebody has brought about 3.000 military able-bodied Turks" - I apologise for the word, but I am quoting - "and has placed them in schools, of the 7.000 that have taken to the woods." And this makes the situation highly complex, and the complete occupation of Zvornik, together with the forces of the front --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, but they were not able to see the actual text on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this is a dramatic appeal and a dramatic caution sent out by the command of the brigade, and it is an accusation of those who are responsible, the superiors, and the fact that in this zone of responsibility there were 3.000 prisoners of war. Whether that fact -- those facts and figures are exact, whether the figures are exact, I don't know because I have not come across them in the study of the documents, in the operative documents and reports. I have not found an exact figure of the prisoners of war and their distribution in the zone of responsibility for the brigade commander at that time to have been -- to have known the exact figure at that time. So this report, which was written on the 18th of July, which is when, based on the documents that I have had at my disposal, was when the whole mass killing had already been completed. The commander of the brigade who would have -- had he taken part in a process of that kind, he would never have left testimony behind him of this kind which absolutely incriminates him and includes him in the chain of responsibility if everything was done in regular fashion. So there is no doubt that this must guide us to looking towards other possibilities of taking part in these serious crimes and violations, and it was outside the system of responsibility of the command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, in your report, you make the firm conviction that General Krstic also is not in the system of responsibility for the crimes that have just been described. They are the crimes that were perpetrated between the 15th and the 18th in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, a little more about why you think that; on the basis of which facts you have made that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My entire work is imbued with that assertion, when I explicitly say it and when it was implicitly implied from my studies and conclusions. I am firmly convinced that General Krstic is not guilty of these crimes for the basic reasons that I have set out. First of all, he has no personal responsibility in the sense of planning, inciting, and encouraging, or personal execution. Second, he did not plan a single document from which we would be able to see a consequence of this kind. Third, General Krstic was the Chief of Staff and, as such, he had no objective command responsibility. On the basis of the doctrine that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was applied by the army of Republika Srpska, relying on the doctrine of the Yugoslav People's Army, the Chief of Staff has command responsibility, direct responsibility, only for his own staff, not for the units, except when he is in command and acting as commander when the commander is not capable of commanding, either for physical reasons he has been incapacitated, for operative reasons, or for being absent from the spot. So in the case of General Krstic, he was somebody who was the chief of staff. He was the Chief of Staff up to the operation at Zepa. From the time the Zepa operation was formulated, that was the 11th of July, General Krstic was taken up with concerns about that particular operation - the preparation of forces, the development of a new command post and its establishment - and spent all his time at a completely separate part, separate area quite apart from the command of the corps and Vlasenica. It is 30 to 40 kilometres away from Vlasenica, and in the zone of responsibility where that occurred, it was 100 kilometres away. So that wouldn't be so relevant if he were the commander of the corps, but he was the commander of the operative group, operational group, for a separate operation. And by virtue of the principle of command and the doctrine of command, he had command authorities for the forces at Zepa of which he was in command and for their conduct and behaviour and their acts or crimes, but not -- possibly, of course, and not for the forces and units of the Drina Corps who were not directly involved in the operation at Zepa right up until the moment he took over his duties as commander and, by that time, everything had been completed. Unfortunately, of course, unfortunately and with regret in this whole complex of the situation around Srebrenica. What happened afterwards, that is the subject of another analysis and not the subject of my own expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, you have responded to my next question with this, but once again, what were the duties in the Drina Corps for General Krstic in July 1995? Could you just enumerate them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic was the chief of the corps staff. He was the commander of the operative group at the source in Zepa, and also he was the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When did General Krstic become the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, General Krstic became the commander of the Drina Corps on the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the usher to prepare Prosecution Exhibit -- Defence Exhibit 151.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, you see the organisation chart of the Drina Corps command structure. Is this command structure of the Drina Corps, was that in place in July in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the organisation chart of the command of the Drina Corps from which you can see that it's -- that it comprises the commander of the corps; the staff of the corps, including the Chief of Staff; then assistant commander for security, with his bodies; then assistant commander for morale, legal, and religious affairs; and also assistant commander for rear services with the entire elements of the logistics and the rear structure and support. So from this you can see that the Chief of Staff was directly in charge and he had the command responsibility towards the Chief of Staff for the security [as interpreted], rear affairs, also for the armoured and mechanised units, also anti-biological and chemical weapons, chief of engineering, chief of artillery and rocket units, chief of communications, chief of anti-aircraft defence, chief of department for personal affairs, and chief of electronic reconnaissance. Also, other organs were not subordinated to the Chief of Staff, so he did not have any command responsibilities towards them. So this is the basic function of the Chief of Staff and his place in the command structure of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In the transcript, line 22, I see that the Chief of Staff has the responsibility -- I see the word here "security." Does the Chief of Staff have any responsibility towards anybody from the Security Services?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He does not have such responsibilities. Only towards the sections that are mentioned in the left -- on the left side of the chart. So he is superior only towards them, and he has the command authority and the command responsibility towards those. The assistant commanders are excepted from that, so the assistant commander for security, assistant commander for political, legal, and religious affairs, and also assistant commander for rear services are not included in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: According to the doctrine applied in the VRS, this system of command is different from the doctrine which was applied in the system of, for example, the armies of the NATO countries. What is the difference in this sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would ask the usher, please, to prepare Prosecution Exhibit 398.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to warn here --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, I apologise. I see here that we do not see the beginning of my question here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My question was, and I will repeat it: In accordance with the doctrine applied in the army of the VRS, the command system is different from the doctrine applied in the system of the armies of the NATO countries. What is the difference in this regard?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had in mind when I was researching the role of the staff in the command functions in our doctrine and also the role of the staff in command functions in the NATO countries, primarily having in mind the testimony of General Dannatt. From this chart that we see on the ELMO, we can see that the corps command is at the head, and there are no other elements in the corps command structure besides the corps, which is directly subordinated to the commander -- the staff, which is directly subordinated to the commander. So that means that the command, under this doctrine, comprises the commander and the staff. In our doctrine, the commands comprise the commander, the staff, and assistant commanders, these three here, but there can be more. For illustration purposes, on one, and the other side, on both sides, assistant commanders, or chiefs, people in charge of security and intelligence, this is unified. So they perform the security functions and also there are people who are in charge of intelligence functions. The difference between our solutions and the other systems is as follows: A person of lower rank, a major, for example -- and I think in the testimony of Mr. Dannatt this was stated that this was a major, but his officers are of lower rank. And you could conclude on the basis of this that these are not officers who are at the same rank as the Chief of Staff, as opposed to that in the command doctrine of the VRS, which has taken that doctrine from the JNA. All of these people who are at the ranks of officers or who are in charge for certain sectors, who are chiefs of departments, their functions -- in their functions, they have high ranks and they are at the same level as the Chief of Staff, so they are at the same level. I think this is an important distinction in order to look at the command functions of the Chief of Staff in the VRS, speaking concretely about the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, which is the subject of our discussion here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: For the record, on Prosecution Exhibit 398, you indicated in the right -- on the right side of the chart the part mentioned -- annotated as COS, which would represent the staff; then G2, which would represent the officers in charge of intelligence and security affairs. I think you stated that that person had the rank of major. Also, at the bottom of this chart, there are two separate people in charge, one for security and one for intelligence affairs, and I think you had said they were captains. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not quite sure whether they are captains, but they are obviously of lower rank than the Chief of Staff, and this is what is important. It is also important to note that the staff structure does not include the assistant commanders, which would include -- which would have the same rank as Chief of Staff. They are all under the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say the staff structures do not follow -- do not include the assistant commander, do you mean the -- do you mean the staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the usher to prepare Prosecution Exhibit 402, footnote 4, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, which regulations guide the command system?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command system is regulated by general regulations, general rules, legal provisions, basic laws which govern relations within the army, as well as special instructions for operative compositions, and especially those that relate to the command functions. A part of the command regulations are contained in the laws governing the army and defence. Explicitly, the problems or the execution of commands is regulated by the rule about the service in the army of Republika Srpska, in the general section of that rule. This is where the principles of superiority are explained, how orders are executed, whose orders are executed, what is the procedure in case orders are not executed. In the rules of service of the army of Republika Srpska also contain a provision on assuming or assumption of duties. This is also regulated: How one assumes duties in tactical units and also how one assumes duties in higher operative units at the strategic level. Besides these regulations, the command system and the principles of command are also regulated in the operative instructions for the corps; in the instruction and rules for the land forces corps, which the army of the Republika Srpska used; also all the instructions that it had at its disposal, which were actually devised in the JNA in 1990. The rules on the -- on authorisational competencies of the corps are also part of the rules which were used and which are used in regulating the command relations. Why is it important for us to know that that part of the regulations is also used in this staff organisation and also in the command system of the Drina Corps, even though it is named "The Rules on Authorisational Competencies in Peacetime"? All the commands, including the command of the Drina Corps, during the entire time of war, were also conducted in the context of peacetime activities. For example, a permanent command post of the Drina Corps was at Vlasenica. In wartime, command posts change places in accordance with the situation that prevails and also in accordance with the type of operations and the area that operations are being conducted in. In the doctrine which static corps -- in the corps, there are static units which receive a specific zone of responsibility in which they spend the entire time of the war, with very little, if any at all, leaving of the area of responsibility. So these activities are carried out as if these were peacetime activities; not combat activities, but non-combat activities. This is why these rules are also important for the Drina Corps in times of war. There is also another instruction that is used, and that is the instructions for the operation of the commands and staff in time of war. This is a provisional instruction. This was made in high military schools of the JNA, but it is also something that is used because it explains how the process of decision-making in planning and preparation of combat activities is carried out, and this is something that is the most important in the activities of a staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we have some problems in finding some exhibits, but let's look at Exhibit 402, footnote 7. The next exhibit is 402, footnote 10, and also footnote 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, yesterday we said something about this document. This is the instruction for the work of 4th Corps command. Could you please turn to page 10 of this instruction. Could you please comment on the duties of the staff and the duties of the Chief of Staff as they are cited in this instruction. If I remember right, you already said yesterday that you had certain reserves towards this instruction and its application.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pages 15 to 17 in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there is any need for me to read the document, it's quite extensive, but I feel compelled to give two comments in respect of this document. I don't think it should be used as an applicable document for the purposes of praising the command responsibility within the Drina Corps and the principle of -- both the principle of responsibility and the factual command authority. What I had in mind was an organisational chart, which this document includes, and where the links between the Chief of Staff and the assistant commanders are established in the way which is not common for the staff organisation to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, General, I think we should perhaps put the chart on the ELMO. I believe we have it in the English version.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I'm talking about here. You see that between the Chief of Staff and the assistant commanders, there is this line which symbolises a firm link, a direct link between the two in the sense of authority and responsibility. Such responsibility, such authority, does not actually exist. That this is an error can be seen from the legend here, from the instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I'm not receiving the interpretation. Something must have happened, either the microphone was not on... Would it be possible for you to repeat this last sentence, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the chart that I have in front of me, there is a legend which explains the links between individual elements within the system of command. This legend makes sense only if the symbols are different and need to be named. However, on this chart, the symbols are identical. There are two possibilities: Either the legend should be left out and we should consider that not all of the symbols which link the individual elements are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Professor Radinovic, but I think that the elements that you were about to show us are not in the English translation. Perhaps you should put your piece of paper on the ELMO and explain to us exactly what you have in mind so that we can follow you. So if you can please tell us what are the elements that we Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have here in the B/C/S version and which cannot be found in the English version. Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, please, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry to interrupt once again. Mr. Visnjic, I have asked the witness to put the B/C/S version on the ELMO so that we can see the difference between the B/C/S version and the English version. So my first question is the following: What is it that we have here in this version that we do not have in the English version? Mr. Visnjic, perhaps you can help us with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the B/C/S version, we have a description of the links existing between the boxes here which contain the description of certain functions; however, all of these links are represented in the same way. So when you read the document, and in particular when you read the English version of the document, which is obvious from the English version, you see that all of the links are of the same nature. I think that the witness is trying to explain to the Chamber that the reality is actually quite opposite; that these links, these relations are not all of the same nature, and that there are two reasons for that; either there had been an error or the person who was drafting this document did not have a basic knowledge of the basic documents or means to represent it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that there is a difference between the two versions. I see that the document that's here on the ELMO has a legend which the English version does not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So you have to tell us what the legend is saying because this is something that we do not have in the English document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Mr. President, I will ask the witness to help us with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please do so, Mr. Visnjic. Ask your question. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, excuse me. In fact, the legend is contained in the English translation. It's on page 13. It's just they couldn't fit it on that document, so it's actually on the next page. That might save some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, because the document that we could see on the ELMO did not have the legend because we could only see the first page of the document. Thank you very much for your assistance, Mr. Cayley. I think that things are clear now. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just about to explain on the chart why this instruction is not in accordance with the doctrine which was applicable at the time in the VRS. This type of linking the Chief of Staff with three remaining assistant commanders implies a conclusion that he has authority in respect of them, towards them, that he is responsible for them, because he is at the same time the Deputy Commander. In accordance with the doctrine which was in force in the VRS, these links here do not exist. The Chief of Staff, as long as he's not acting as the commander, he has no authority whatsoever towards assistant commanders, and that is the crucial difference. So this should have been in this way: Without these links here between the assistant commanders and the Chief of Staff, because the Chief of Staff did not have any command competences over them. It is only by virtue of his function as Deputy Commander, when he becomes the commander, at that point he has authority over assistant commanders. And that is why I said that this instruction, this chart, should not be used while assessing the command responsibility of the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Radinovic, I should like to ask the assistance of the usher and to have him put the English version of the chart on the ELMO, please, and also the following page, page 13, which includes the legend. Mr. President, if you will allow me a brief explanation at this point. In the chart that we have in the English version, all of the links are depicted as same links, of the same type; however, in the legend, we see that we have three different types of links, that there should be three different types of lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, you are now looking at the English version. Tell us whether all of the links between the separate commands and departments that we can see here on page 12 of the English version, are they of the same kind, of the same nature?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they're not. The links between the commander and the Chief of Staff and his three assistant commanders and all of the units that are immediately subordinate to them, this is the actual link of command authority. The dotted line that we have here represents the type of relationships, which implies cooperation. So we do not have direct command link here. The Chief of Staff has authority over his staff, not over the assistant commanders. There should be a dotted line here so that you know that, functionally speaking, the Chief of Staff actually coordinates the work of the command in the functional sense, not in the command sense. And that is the crucial difference that I wanted to draw your attention to because, in this way, you end up gaining a completely different picture about the command responsibility of the Chief of Staff. Looking from this chart, one would conclude that the Chief of Staff has command responsibility over all elements of the command at any point in time, which he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, would you please turn to page 10 of the B/C/S version of the same document, that is, the instruction to the 4th Corps command, Exhibit number 402, footnote 7; and if you can give us your brief comment of this document.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 10 of the instructions to the 4th Corps command, we have the authorities and competences of the certain elements of the command, both individually speaking and for the staff in general. This instruction significantly expands the authority -- the competence of the staff, and modifies the authority and the responsibilities of the staff which are defined within the rules of Land Forces Corps, which are applicable for all corps. This is a far more -- this is a broader instruction, this one here, and I think that here we have a document which actually follows from the general rules of Land Forces Corps because here we have a specific corps in mind, namely, the 4th Sarajevo Corps. They are not allowed, entitled, to modify the essence of the command -- of the system of the command as it is described for the level -- at the level of the corps which is applicable to all, that is, the rule of the Land Forces Corps. This is important because, when assessing the function of the staff, and of course, on the basis of that, assessing the responsibility of the Chief of Staff - in case in point, it is General Krstic - so this responsibility in the reports of Mr. Butler and Mr. Dannatt is expanded. It is broadened in accordance with this instruction to the 4th Corps command. In my report and here during my testimony, I should like to point out that we should go back to the original document which clearly indicates the nature of the role of the Chief of Staff, and we should not base ourselves on this particular document because here that role is significantly changed and modified.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I should like to suggest that we go back to the original document, that is, the Prosecution Exhibit 402, footnote 4, that is, the rules of Land Forces Corps.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, let us have a look at the Prosecution Exhibit 402, footnote 10, then, Instructions to the Rules of Land Forces Corps in Peacetime. I think you have this provisional rules. Very well, then, this is the document that we were looking for.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 34, paragraph 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, you said that that was the document that you were looking for. You mean document P402, footnote 2 or footnote 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm just checking. It is the document 404 - I'm sorry. I'm sorry - document 402, footnote 4. That is the document entitled "Rule Corps of Ground Forces (Provisional)."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that was the document that you were looking for and that could not be found? There has been a miracle, apparently. I hope you can now continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, this document that we see here, is that the document that you consider to be the original document when it comes to the determination of the duties and functions of the staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Page 34 in the Serbian version, in paragraph 66, we can read as follows: "Staff is the principal body of the Corps Command which functionally connects and integrates the work of all bodies of the command," that is, functionally speaking. It is headed by the Chief of Staff, who is at the same time Deputy Commander of the Corps. And it goes on: "He is the only one who, in keeping with the Commander's decision," so not without the decision or contrary to the decision, "has the right to give assignments to subordinates." And then it goes on with the composition and the make-up of the staff. So the corps -- 4th Corps had no right whatsoever to provide for anything other than the functional command of the Chief of Staff in respect of assistant commanders. So this is the relevant provision which authorises the Chief of Staff to coordinate the work of the staff and to have command responsibility over assistant commanders only in keeping with the commander's decision.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Exhibit number 401, please, which is a report on the command responsibility of the corps in the VRS, submitted by Mr. Butler. And I should like to ask the witness -- actually, I should like to ask the usher to place paragraph 2.0 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, can we please hear your comment of the paragraph 2.0, that is, the last portion of the paragraph. And if you can please tell the Chamber whether you agree with the position adopted by Mr. Butler; and if not, why?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this simply is the consequence of a different interpretation, a different understanding of the command structure and the role of the staff within that command structure. When Mr. Butler defines the role of the Corps Commander - that is also one part of his report - in the third paragraph in this item he says that he is personally, directly, and legally empowered to, and then he goes on to quote, "... lead the operations of the Corps Command, assign tasks to his subordinate officers, ensure that they are carried out and bear full responsibility for their completion," with which I completely agree. This quotation ends and the text goes on: "The Corps Commander accomplishes this," that is, he commands, "by exercising military command and control, either directly or through a body of subordinates, subordinate officers, assistants, and branch specialists, referred to as the Corps Staff." So for Mr. Butler, assistant commanders are members of the staff, which is not the case in accordance with our doctrine. So in accordance with the doctrine of the JNA, which was adopted also by the VRS, assistant commanders are not members of the staff, but branch specialists are members of the staff. So that is one difference, the other one being that the command within the corps is never exercised indirectly, but directly. So within the staff, the command is always direct. The commander does not anyone below him who would take over his order and transmit it further down [as interpreted]. The command is carried out in a direct manner between the one issuing the order and the individual who is supposed to carry out the order. The commander issues, in a direct manner, orders to his immediate subordinates, that is, brigade commanders and commanders of independent battalions. There is no intermediary in this line of command. However, there can be some kind of indirect command, but only in the functional sense - if one is supposed to, for example, draft an auxiliary order, supporting material of some kind, if a document needs to be articulated or explained in any specific manner - but that is also specifically provided for. There is an activity which is referred to as command reconnaissance. That kind of work refers to the decision of the commander in battlefield. His decision in that case is transmitted to his subordinates, who are in charge of seeing to that the decision is in accordance with the reality in the ground. That doesn't mean that the command within the structure is not direct. The command is always carried out in a direct manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to show us paragraph 2.8 and to put the relevant page on the ELMO, please. For the record, it is the same exhibit, Prosecution Exhibit 401.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, please, your comment on the conclusion made by Mr. Butler in paragraph 2.8.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 2.8, we read that: "The Corps Staff, under the direction of the Chief of Staff, is responsible for reviewing and understanding the assigned directives received by the Superior Command." I think that this must be an error in translation. I don't think that Mr. Butler would make such a mistake and such an omission, because his report is indeed of a very high quality. I don't think that he could have made such a mistake. So that is why I'm drawing your attention to this particular bit of the text. I think it needs to be corrected. No one can issue directives to the Superior Command. It is the Superior Command that issues directives. That is why I believe that this was a mistake in translation. And there is also one other sentence that I would like to comment on: "As soon as the commander approves the general concept." I have to say that the commander does not have to approve the concept. The concept is his. He can consult with his assistant commanders and his departments as regards the implementation of his general concept. However, the general concept or the basic concept is the product of the work of the commander, and not anyone else. Everybody has to obey, listen to the general concept issued by the commander, and once they receive, once they have been notified of that general concept, they go on with their relevant functions in respect of that general concept. Once the overall concept and the operations plans are approved by the commander, the corps staff then transmits the decision, orders to the subordinate commands. If we have in mind paragraph 66 of the Rules of Land Forces Corps, that is, the corps for ground forces, we see that this far exceeds the responsibility and the authority of the Chief of Staff, which is provided for in paragraph 66 of the Corps of Armed Forces Rule, which is a general document applicable to all corps, not only to the 4th Corps. So the staff does not transmit the decision. The staff is in charge of preparing the plan of the operation in accordance with the decision of the commander, and the commander is the one who issues the order to his subordinate units, without any intermediaries. He communicates directly with them, either in oral manner or in written manner, but there is no, once again, any intermediary in the sense of command. And it does not become responsible for controlling the implementation of the plan or orders. Every assistant commander is duty-bound and responsible for the execution of the decision of the commander within his department. It is not the Chief of Staffs who is responsible for all of the departments. He is only responsible for the departments which are actually part of the staff. So that was my remark, my criticism, and also my indication as to how we should understand this, because we will have problems if we follow the instructions to the 4th Corps command and not the general Rules of Land Forces Corps when it comes to the responsibility and the authority of the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want to ask General Radinovic a clarification. Just for my knowledge, you said nobody issues orders to the Superior Command. Is the Superior Command the head of the state? Do you mean by that the head of the state?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher turn the document to paragraph 2.12. It is still Prosecution Exhibit 401.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, could you comment on paragraph 2.12.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this paragraph, in the first sentence, first line, it says -- it is the same context, of course, but it would perhaps be a good idea for us to clarify matters so that we have the same groundwork for interpreting this. Despite the presence of assistant -- despite the presence of assistant commanders of possibly equal rank on the corps staff, only the Chief of Staff is empowered to issue orders. So responsibility of the Chief of Staff is different if the assistant commanders are in the staff. They are not in the staff, corps staff. And the continuation of that sentence says that, despite the fact that in the corps staff there are assistant commanders and so on, which can be of the same rank or higher rank, it is only the Chief of Staff who is empowered to issue orders to the entire corps staff, to include branch bodies and services. So it is not the Chief of Staff that issues orders either to the assistant for security or to the assistant for the rear or the assistant for moral guidance and religious questions. They are issued orders exclusively by the commander, not by the Chief of Staff. And it goes on to say, "to subordinate formations of the corps." Not even to the subordinate formations of the corps does the Chief of Staff issue orders, except in situations where he is in charge of commanding the corps, which means when the commander is not on the spot to do so. And he does so always in the name of the commander; not as the Chief of Staff, but he does so in the name of the commander in the commander's absence. So those are essential differences, vital differences. I don't know if I've been able to explain this to you well enough, explain the difference between the two; but it is a vital difference, and it throws quite a different light on the whole question of command responsibility if you explain the role of the staff, corps staff, and the Chief of Staff in this way. And it should not be explained as it exists in this document but as it is regulated in the source document, that is to say, in the rule relating to ground forces dating from 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that this would be a good moment to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree with you, Mr. Visnjic. Let us take a break, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the interpretation service has -- the translation service has drawn my attention to some inconsistencies in the translation, so before we go back to Prosecution Exhibit 398 -- that is, can we go back to 398, please. And it concerns a description of the functions given by General Radinovic, so I'd like to ask the General to describe this once again to us, to explain it once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Trial Chamber, this is the diagram of the NATO country forces' corps command, and below the division command, what are the other boxes and what functions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Below the division commander, we have the Chief of Staff, and underneath the Chief of Staff is his assistant for intelligence and security. On this example, we can see the difference between staff as conceived in British military doctrine and corps staff in our own doctrine. The assistant for security is not the assistant to the Chief of Staff in our doctrine. He is assistant to the commander; whereas in British doctrine, he is assistant to the Chief of Staff. This shows that the structure of the staff and roles of the staff are not identical in both the doctrines, and that is what I would like to draw your attention to and insist upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And for purposes of the interpretation once again and translation, what do we have underneath the G2 box?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is different, too, than it is in our own doctrine. In order to analyse command responsibility, this is not such an essential point. The function of security and intelligence has been conjoined in this staff here, in this box, and the assistant to the Chief of Staff for intelligence and security affairs has his own assistant for security and for intelligence as well. As can be seen from the diagram which depicts the corps staff in our doctrine, corps command in our own doctrine, the chief of intelligence, the assistant of the Chief of Staff for security matters, he is assistant to the commander. He is not a member of the staff but is assistant to the commander and ranks on a par with the Chief of Staff. And that, indeed, is an essential difference. It is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask the usher to present the witness with Prosecution 402, footnote 10. It is the rule, rules of -- regulations on the responsibilities of the land army corps command in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, could you turn to page 7 of the regulations - actually, it is page 8 in the English version - and could you comment on the application of these regulations, that is to say, whether it can be applied to the concrete situation in respect of the functions of the Chief of Staff in the corps in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article relates to the functioning of the commands in peacetime, the regulations refer to that; and they regulate the competencies of the Chief of Staff in peacetime, and that is all right. That is all in order. But in view of the fact that many of the functions of command from 1992, November 1992 when the Drina Corps was established up until the end of the war or up to 1995, which is what interests us, in the zone of responsibility, this was done; and it was comparable to the conditions that prevailed in peacetime because there was -- fighting did not go on all the time. Combat and fighting was periodical, and therefore it did not affect the entire zone of responsibility. On the contrary, in most cases, the combat activities took place only in a small portion of the zone of responsibility, whereas in the rest of the area of responsibility, life went on as normal, we might say, just as if there wasn't a war, of course with all the consequences that a wartime encirclement had. I'm thinking of shortages, so there were shortages and everything else that is attached to wartime. But this is in keeping fully with paragraph 66 of the rules for the corps of ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, could you tell the Trial Chamber a more detailed explanation and your views of the relationship between the commander of the Drina Corps, the Chief of Staff, or Deputy Commander of the Drina Corps, the relationships between these functions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The areas of command are very precisely defined when it comes to this question. The commander, Corps Commander, does not share his command responsibility with anybody at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I cannot see your response here on the transcript. I cannot see that your answer is being recorded on the LiveNote. We need an "A" for answer. We have the "Q" for question, but we need "A" for answer. Could you give us your answer again, please? Could you start again?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those relationships are very precisely and clearly defined and regulated. The commander of the corps does not share his command competency with anybody, or command responsibility with anybody. All the people in the staff and in the command - that is to say, the Chief of Staff and his three assistants - when the commander is there on the spot, they function as his assistants. It is only the Chief of Staff, in the absence of the commander, by way of automatism, takes over the function of command because, according to the rules and regulations and according to the law, it is provided for the fact that he then acts as deputy commander, as deputy commander. So that provision is there so that in no situation whatsoever is there any discontinuity in command. A solution of this kind liberates the commander of the responsibility that when he is absent, when he is prevented from being on the spot, he does not have to write out an act or document designating a deputy. So the Chief of Staff, on the basis of this automatic mechanism, takes over in the absence of the commander, when the commander is absent for any reason whatsoever and is incapable of command, physically, spatially, professionally, or for any reason whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask the usher -- I should like to ask the usher to have the witness shown Prosecution Exhibit 403. Exhibit 403 is Mr. Butler's report. Could the usher please turn to paragraph 8.43, 8.43. That is the paragraph we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, sir --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you just allow me a few moments to find it for myself as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, what was the role and responsibility of General Krstic in the Krivaja 95 operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of General Krstic in the Krivaja 95 operation was the role of Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps and, at the same time, deputy commander. In his role of Chief of Staff of the corps, he was duty-bound --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we're having a problem. I think we ought to take the document off the ELMO because it is marked "confidential." Have you any indications to that effect, Mr. Visnjic? Is this a confidential document indeed? That is what the registrar is -- Madam Registrar has just told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, Mr. President, this is a public document, but let me consult my learned colleagues of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's a public document, this document. It's Mr. Butler's military narrative from Operation Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, where did you get that marking from?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might, I think the problem may be this: 400/3 is a document that's under seal. 403 is this document, which is not under seal. So there may be a slash missing. That's perhaps where the confusion is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're now -- as far as I remember, it is document 403; is that right? And the other document, 400/3, was under seal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Madam Registrar did draw my attention to this. Thank you very much. You try to be of assistance. But without losing more time, let us proceed, Mr. Visnjic. We have the document on the ELMO, and I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, what was the role and responsibility of General Krstic in Operation Krivaja 95?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said in starting my response, General Krstic, in Operation Krivaja 95, was at the post of Chief of Staff. He was -- and also deputy commander. He was also the deputy of the commander. And his role at that post was to plan the Operation Krivaja 95 and, from the forward command post, as Chief of Staff, to supervise its implementation, the course of the operation, and, in keeping with the course of the operation, to propose to the commander the undertaking of measures in keeping with the development of the situation on the ground. In his role of deputy commander of the Drina Corps, General Krstic could have, when the Corps Commander was not around, then he could have realised the function of command. Furthermore, General Krstic, together with the commander, was at the forward command post at Pribicevac, and always, at all times when at that command spot the commander was absent, he could have the right to command units in that operation. But let me repeat, only in the absence of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, would you now take a look at Exhibit 403, paragraph 8.43, and give us your comments with respect to what Mr. Butler says.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a summary, a precis of Mr. Butler's findings, and in the paragraph C 8.43, he says as follows: "In reviewing the period prior to 13 July 1995, it is clear that General-Major Krstic was not only functioning as the Drina Corps Chief of Staff, but he was probably also functioning as the," and then it says in inverted commas, "`operational commander' for the military forces grouped together for Operation Krivaja 95." This assertion is not incorrect, but its intentions are such that they demand comment, merit comment. I don't know what "operational commander" written in inverted commas actually means, but I wish to stress that this -- a syntagma of this kind is not used in the doctrine of command of the Yugoslav People's Army. It is not something that the JNA used, and therefore the army of Republika Srpska didn't use it either. A commander can only be an operational commander. He cannot be an inoperational commander or the opposite of "operational." I don't know how to interpret the real meaning of this syntagma used here, "operational commander," and even less so what it means in the sense of command competence and command responsibility of General Krstic. He, at the forward command post of the corps performing an operation, engaged in an operation, he was there at the forward command post, and he was always in the role of Chief of Staff there, except in situations when the Corps Commander was unable to command, exercise his function of command. And this instance -- in these instances, he commanded completely, in full, as if he were commander, without any restrictions, and he is authorised to do so by his -- by virtue of his function of Deputy Commander. And therefore, there is no need to use any metaphors which can cloud the issue and present his role in an erroneous light. So as Deputy Commander, he commands in the full sense of the word with all the command competencies in the absence of the commander, and no papers or documents are necessary for him to receive additional authorisation of that kind. By definition, he is the commander in the absence of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, how do you view the position and function of General Krstic at the time of the moving out of the population from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic, as I have already said, at the time the population moved out from Potocari, was the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps and, at the same time, Deputy Commander. When this problem arose and when it had to be solved, General Krstic received the task of planning, organising, and executing a new operation, and that new operation was the operation at Zepa. That was his assignment. It is within the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, but it is in the south of the zone. At the moment when he received -- when he took on this new role, General Krstic started the planning of that particular operation. As we can see from the acts and documents, of the testimonies -- and testimony before this Tribunal, we can learn that from the commander of the Main Staff, he was appointed commander of the operative group for the preparation and for the implementation of the operation at Zepa. Therefore, he was appointed commander. Now, we can ask ourselves whether that was absolutely necessary in view of the fact that he was the Deputy Commander already and, therefore, was in a position to command the forces at Zepa without receiving any separate decree on appointment. Of course he could have. That is another way it could have been done. But the commander of the Main Staff assessed that this was a different axis, a separate axis, and that it was necessary to have a commander who would be in charge of that operation. And what is more important, that the Corps Commander, that is to say the nominal Corps Commander, should be excluded and liberated from his command responsibility and authorisation and competence for part of the forces of the Corps taking part and engaged in the Zepa operation. Therefore, by appointing -- by this appointment, the commander of the Main Staff fully transmitted all command responsibility to the commander of the operative group and excluded the commander of the Drina Corps from having that responsibility. Why he did that, it is difficult to say with any certainty now. All the more so as we do not have any statements by the people who actually made the decision. All I can do is to speculate. I can assume that he evaluated the situation, and that from the 11th of July in the evening, two parallel and two very major operational problems occurred in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, and that it would have been difficult for one man, one person, one individual to cover both these situations, that is to say, both these major events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say, "by this appointment, the commander of the Main Staff fully transmitted all command responsibility to the commander of the operative group and excluded the commander of the Drina Corps from having any responsibility" - that is what you said, it is in the LiveNote, in the record - which responsibility were you referring to as excluding the commander? That is to say, what responsibility was left to the command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that the commander of the Drina Corps, the command Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the Main Staff relieved of the responsibility of preparing and leading the operation at Zepa and all the consequences that could result from that. At the same time, he retained the commander responsibility for problems which arose in the zone of responsibility in the Srebrenica region and the region of Potocari, and in the whole area of responsibility outside the region where the Zepa operation was conducted. To the contrary, the appointment would have no sense at all, there would be no meaning to the appointment, because General Krstic could have commanded the forces at Zepa even without that appointment by virtue of the automatic mechanism that stepped in because, in Zivanovic's absence, Krstic could command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, could you explain to the Trial Chamber in greater detail the role of General Krstic in Operation Stupcanica 95, or let us -- let me ask it a different way. What does Stupcanica 95 mean? And at the same time, I should like to ask the usher to prepare Prosecution Exhibit 425 for us, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stupcanica is the coded name for the operation for Zepa. I stated yesterday in my testimony that it was the practice either to name operations by using well-known toponyms or terms which have some clear message, such as "storm," "desert storm," "flash." So the proper name "Stupcanica" - and since we're discussing this question, I made a lapse, small lapse yesterday, so I would like for this to be kept in mind. When I was talking about operations nominated in directive 7, I said that Operation Spreca was not carried out. I meant the strategic operations. So they were not carried out nor executed. So this operation Sprecanica [phoen], on the contact of the East Bosnian and Drina Corps, this should also have been carried out with East Bosnian Corps and also together in cooperation with the Drina Corps. This operation was planned and started, but it was not carried out. And what is the strangest thing in this whole complex is that nobody was actually held accountable for that. And actually, the Drina Corps [as interpreted] had 37 casualties as a result of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking now about directive number 7 in Exhibit 425. Could we look at page 7 of the Serbian version. I just wanted to correct the transcript, line 18. It is stated that the Drina Corps had 37, but actually we're talking about the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let us come back to directive number 7. General Radinovic, do you find a basis in this directive for Operation Stupcanica 95?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is no basis for this operation here. The Drina Corps was meant to carry out operation Zvijezda, Spreca, Prozor [indiscernible] 95, but obviously there is no Operation Stupcanica. However, in this same directive, Krivaja 95 is mentioned, but in a different way. Krivaja 95 is not mentioned regarding the Drina Corps; it's mentioned regarding another corps, and that is the Herzegovina Corps, Herzegovina Corps, and the region of operation --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Could you please make a break between the question and the answer, because I see here in the transcript it's not clear where the question ends and the answer begins, so I will ask the question again. Is there -- is Krivaja 95, the Operation Krivaja 95, mentioned in directive 7?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's mentioned, but not for the Drina Corps, but for the Herzegovina Corps. The area where Krivaja 95 is supposed to be carried out in directive number 7 for the Herzegovina Corps is the valley of the River Drina [as interpreted] -- Neretva, but this is not in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, I must intervene once again. So the Krivaja 95 operation that is mentioned in directive 7 is the region of the River Neretva, and not Drina, as it states in the transcript. I think he's already brought back the document, but if the usher could please place on the ELMO the page where Krivaja 95 is mentioned in directive number 7, in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think it's the page before, Mr. President. I think if you turn one page back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that Mr. Cayley did not look on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It's right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, we're talking about pages 12 and 13 in the English translation, relating to the Herzegovina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So Krivaja 95, which is mentioned in this directive, has nothing to do with Krivaja 95, which was actually carried out?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It has nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, there are a number of interpretations - this Trial Chamber has heard several versions - and interpretations of when General Krstic became commander of the Drina Corps. When do you believe General Krstic became the commander of the Drina Corps, and why do you believe that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that General Krstic became the commander of the Drina Corps on the 20th of July, 1995. I believe that this was -- that he became the commander on that date because on that day he assumed his duties at a meeting which was attended by the commanders of some corps, assistant commanders of the Main Staff, and representatives of some civilian structures of power. And this was the way it was planned, or this is provided for under the rules of service in the army of Republika Srpska regarding the transfer and assumption of duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to prepare Prosecution Exhibit 468.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, who appointed General Krstic, and under -- in which document, as the commander of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic was appointed commander of the Drina Corps by a decree of the president of Republika Srpska, who is the only authorised person for these kind of appointments. So the president of Republika Srpska appointed the commander of the Drina Corps to his duties, Major-General Radislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We have that document. This is Prosecution Exhibit 468. My question -- for the record, I have to start again. I don't see in the transcript -- I don't see the question in the transcript, the "Q" indicating that the question has begun. We have before us Prosecution Exhibit 468. How should we understand these dates based on the principles of military doctrine? How do we interpret the dates from this decree?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of Republika Srpska by a decree registered under number 011369/95 named General Krstic as commander of the Drina Corps on July 14th, 1995. But at the bottom of the document itself there is a statement saying that he and Colonel Andric, who was to take over the duties of the Chief of Staff of the corps, will be appointed as of July 15th, 1995. So the president of the Republic, who is the only person authorised to appoint commanders at that level, has said -- or set July 15th as the date when General Krstic is permitted, I stress "permitted," to take over his duties. Before that date, he should not or he is not permitted to take over such duties. So that is the date as of which General Krstic can/may take over his duties, if we keep in mind that the taking on and the handing over of responsibility is a process and not just an act. So the president of the Republic does not set a certain date by which he has to take over his responsibility because conditions need to be created for this. Which conditions are we talking about? General Krstic at that time was carrying out operations in Zepa, and this was a very complicated, difficult, comprehensive action, so that there was no question that General Krstic could have dealt with anything else except that operation right up until the operation was not [as translated] completed or until there is an operative pause which would create the conditions for him to take over his duties. What makes it easier in this whole process to take over responsibility is the fact that we are talking about a superior officer who is familiar with the corps, who knows the situation, who before his appointment would occasionally perform the function of Corps Commander when the nominal commander was not in a position to carry out his command function. So for him to take over his duties, it was not essential to have the usual or the customary period of time that is usually provided for newly-appointed commanders, when we're talking about a person, an officer who is from another unit, from another zone of responsibility, when such a person assumes a new and a terrain that is not familiar enough to him, and also when he comes into a new operative and tactical situation which he is not very well acquainted with. So for General Krstic, we only needed some kind of operative pause, a kind of respite in the Zepa operation so that he could then take over his duties. In accordance with the circumstances, this took place on August 20th with the presence of numerous corps officers, commanders, deputy commanders, and also this took place in the presence of a certain number of civil authorities, representatives. So this is a ceremony where it is practically announced that there is a new person who will be in command of the corps. Was there any need to rush with this? I think not. Perhaps it was even possible to wait for the operation to be completely finished, and then when the forward command post was again withdrawn to the basic command post in Vlasenica, then they could have perhaps carried out the handover and the taking over. Well, perhaps there are certain reasons why this was required. This was something that I did not deal with, but I believe that there was no reason to rush and I would not wish to speculate why this happened, but it is undoubtedly that this took place on the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, I see a certain date in the transcript, so I will ask you this question again. When did General Krstic take over the duties of commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic took over the duties of Corps Commander on July 20th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I would like to correct -- this was probably just a slip of the tongue, we're talking about page 44, line 6, the date "August" is mentioned, so that is the reason why I asked this question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, when we're talking about the act of taking over, handing over and taking over duties, this is something that is provided for in the regulations of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is regulated by the rules of service of the army of Republika Srpska in a section which is called "Assumption of Duties." This, of course, pertains to taking over duties in peacetime, so this is in cases of taking over of duty in peacetime. In tactical units, the assumption of duties is carried out in front of a line-up of soldiers from the bottom right up to the top ranks of the army, including the Deputy Commanders or assistant commanders of the Main Staff. And the Chiefs of Staffs of the corps and officers at their level, they assume their duties at a working meeting of the corps command, i.e., in the presence at that level at which the handing over of duties is performed. This is where the handing over of duties and the taking on of duties is officially carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, during your research, did you ever come across any documents, any statements which would indicate that between the 13th, 15th, and the 20th of July, 1995, that there was -- that there were some exceptional circumstances which would require the application of that automatic mechanism in the takeover of duty between the Chief of Staff and the Corps Commander as part of the function of the Chief of Staff, the mechanism that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't find any such circumstances, the existence of any such circumstances which would require the procedure of takeover of duty to be speeded up. Quite the contrary. The circumstances pointed to the fact that the handover of duty should have been postponed until the completion of the Zepa operation. There was no need whatsoever for that procedure to take over on the 20th. But this is just my analytical assessment from a distance. Most probably, it was possible to complete the procedure on the 20th. And of course, there was an obligation which was contained in the decree of the president of the 15th of July, so the procedure had to take place sometime. Whether it had to take place on that particular date or not, I don't know. It's a matter of practical circumstances which I don't know anything about. I haven't come across any circumstances, any situation which would indicate the need to speed up the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Professor Radinovic, I think that you testified today that the law provided for the Chiefs of Staff to be able to replace automatically, without any written document, the Corps Commander. Was that the case here? You say that it was not necessary to speed up the procedure of takeover of duty. In particular, was one of the reasons for that the fact that, in accordance with the law, he was -- he could act as the Deputy Commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, no, we cannot interpret it that way. He is not the commander according to the law. According to the law, he's only Deputy Commander, and that obligation, that right, is contained in his post, in his function of the Chief of Staff. So in addition to his post as the Chief of Staff, he is also Deputy Commander, and he can exercise the command over the entire corps only in the absence or unavailability of the commander. However, he does not have all of the rights pertaining to the function of the Corps Commander, except, of course, when the commander is not there. The president of the Republic probably had certain reasons in mind when he appointed General Krstic Corps Commander, and to appoint the outgoing, the former Corps Commander, to some other post. That is his discretional right, and I do not have enough information, enough knowledge on the basis of which I could tell you the reasons that led the president of the Republic to appoint him to that post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you come across any indication, any particular circumstances during your research which would indicate that Commander Zivanovic was not able -- that it was impossible for him to exercise his role of the commander?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I haven't come across that piece of information, that is, the information which would indicate that he was unable or prevented from fulfilling his duty, the duty of the Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. I think that we can continue until 10 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just a question, General Radinovic. You just mentioned in passing that maybe the president of the Republic had special reasons for appointing General Krstic this post.
