Was it - I mean, in the army - was it some kind of natural grades going higher and higher? Was it time for him to be put in this post or was he, as you said, there were some special reasons to put him, some exceptional reasons?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there was any exceptional reason. Had it existed, I would have probably known about it and I would have mentioned it in my testimony and my report as well. However, according to what I know, I don't think that there was such a reason and that there was any need for this procedure to be speeded up. They could have waited for a lull in the conduct of operations and have the procedure conducted in the usual relaxed way. It is his right, the right of the president of the Republic, to appoint generals to such high positions, such as the position of the Corps Commander. It is a discretional right of the president to do that. I'm not a legal expert. I don't know what that right entails. But there is a normal way of advancing through the chain. There are special schools, special courses to that effect, and certain criteria for fulfilling the function of the Corps Commander are explicitly set and there is a number of other requirements that need to be fulfilled for someone to be appointed to that position. And I believe that there was enough time and enough opportunity to see whether General Krstic would be able to fulfil all of those conditions and requirements, and I believe that with his conduct, with his experience, and also thanks to his function as the Chief of Staff, was quite legitimately named to the post of the Corps Commander, whether on the 14th of July or whether on the 25th. He would have been appointed to that position in -- by any such decree, but I don't know the reasons why he was appointed by this particular decree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So excuse me. Were there other senior officers eligible, more eligible than him, for this post?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is very difficult for me, Your Honour, to answer your question. I believe that there was, but if you are now going to ask me for a specific name, specific person, I wouldn't know. I would have to think about that a little bit, and I could perhaps come up with a list of people who might be eligible. However, in the VRS, and the JNA, from which I come, and General Krstic as well, it is perfectly natural for an officer to advance, and it is perfectly customary for the commander to be succeeded by his Chief of Staff, that is, the person who had already had experience acting as the Corps Commander and who would be best placed to do so in the future. I know that General Dannatt mentions something to that effect in his report. I might be mistaken, and I apologise if that is the case, but I believe that he said that in the army of the United Kingdom, a commander -- another officer is appointed to the post of the commander, someone coming from the outside, which is not such a bad idea, because it makes it possible for the professional relationships to function in a better way. Because if you have a too personal situation, a too personal atmosphere, that can complicate things in terms of profession. But however, this is how things work in the army that I am familiar with, and I cannot comment further on in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just what made me ask you that question was that you said that the president might have some special reasons to appoint him, that's all. So if you don't know the special reasons, all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: General, we have a saying, which you may be familiar with, that you don't change horses in the middle of the stream. And in your military experience -- Yes. I'm sure it's a universal notion. In your military experience, is it not exceptional to -- for the president, the Supreme Commander, to change the commander of a corps at a time when, you have so adroitly pointed out, the corps was faced with two major operations: one the Zepa operation and one the -- whatever the clean-up or whatever the follow-up was in the Srebrenica. And President Karadzic's decree is -- came down on the 14th. It said, "effective on the 15th." I know you've explained what your interpretation of "effect" is, but was that not in itself unusual to bring that change down in the middle of two crises, as it were, for the corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can answer your question only conditionally speaking, and let me say the reasons why. I don't know -- I'm not familiar with the general situation and the context in which that particular decree was made. It is a practice, when it comes to the high levels of command, that certain types of legal documents and appointment decisions, including appointments for high commanding posts, are made in certain conditions and given a certain temporal time framework. It is perfectly customary for those individuals to be discussed and assessed during certain high-level meetings, and it is quite possible that the appointment in question was a kind of epilogue of an assessment of the personnel situation, human resources situation, and the service in charge of drafting such documents then prepare the relevant document on the 14th. I don't see any other reason for that. Frankly speaking, I -- that particular fact didn't lead me to any specific research as to why that was the case. But I fully agree with you when you say that you don't change horses in the middle of the stream.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Professor. I also have a question concerning the issue that is being discussed. Do you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. know who General Zivanovic replaced in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know, Your Honour. I'm sorry for having failed to pay attention to that particular fact. I consider it to be my personal omission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have another question for you, General. You said that it was not necessary to speed up the procedure of takeover of duty of General Krstic. Can you tell us: Do you know why it was urgent for General Krstic [as interpreted] to be promoted, why that promotion was a matter of urgency?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. I don't know. Because somehow I don't think that General Zivanovic later on took up any significant post on the basis of which I would remember him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also said that the president of Republika Srpska had availed himself of his right in discretionary manner. Do you know if he was adequately informed of the time and of the operations that were taking place at the time when he signed the decree on the promotion of Zivanovic? Because I understand that he has a discretionary right to do that, but I don't think that he would have done that in an arbitrary fashion. He must have had some good reasons for that. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I tried to explain to you the way in which these personnel issues are dealt with and on the basis of what relevant documents are issued, in view of the practice in the VRS and the JNA, and I think that the procedure is similar to the procedure applied in any other army. There wasn't any single urgent reason for that replacement, as far as I know, in my judgement. I don't think that it was urgent for General Zivanovic to take up this new post. And if there had been something very important, if there had been some kind of crisis of a sort, I think I would have known that, because I studied the matter in detail, from a safe distance, of course, from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, from Belgrade. But I know that there was no need for General Krstic to be moved from his duty of the commander of the operational group in Zepa until such time as that operation is completed. So I cannot answer you with any precision as to why that was done at that particular point in time. It is perfectly obvious that that change in personnel was the result of the status of General Krstic, his experience, his previous service, and the time that he spent serving as the Chief of Staff of the corps. So that solution in itself is perfectly natural and motivated. As to why it was done on the 14th of July, why the decree is dated the 14th of July, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is a convenient time for a break, Mr. Visnjic. Were you about to say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But you will have to trust me, but -- for this particular matter. I think, then, on page 51, line 13, the name stated is General Krstic instead of General Zivanovic, but you will have to trust me, as I say, because it's no longer on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. We will see that. I think that we should now have our usual lunch break, which will take -- which will last 50 minutes today, because we will then have to divide the remaining working time in two blocks. So we will come back at 5 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I have one more question for the witness before you continue. General Radinovic, you told us, and we already knew, that General Krstic commanded the Zepa operation according to the rules, according to the customs and standard practice of the VRS and other armies. So what we have is at the same time we have General Mladic, the chief of the Main Staff, and then we have General Zivanovic as commander of the Drina Corps, and General Krstic as the Chief of Staff. In normal conditions, if I can use that term, according to the rules, according to customs, according to your knowledge, who should have commanded the Zepa operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have the undeniable fact as to who commanded the operation at Zepa, and that was General Krstic. He commanded it. Now, I could, of course, speculate as to who should have been in command, but that's another matter. And it was a legitimate order, a legitimate -- a completely legitimate decision that the most prominent officer from the Corps command should command the forces in an operation which was not a very -- one of a very broad scale. It wasn't a broad-scale operation which would require the engagement of all available -- of all -- the whole potential of the Drina Corps, and in that case, it would have been natural that, at the forward command post in Krivace, we have the commander of the Drina Corps present as well. So the commander of the Main Staff, I can only assume, weighed things up and thought that the most productive solution, the best solution, was to separate the Corps Commander and his deputy, that is to say, his Chief of Staff, and that the Deputy Commander of the Drina Corps should be explicitly, by decree, given the role of commander of the operative group; and the commander of the Drina Corps should be left with the competencies over all the other problems that might occur within the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps. And already on the 11th of July, it was quite clear that two major operational problems and humanitarian problems would arise in the zone of responsibility, and that was to see to and move out, on the basis of the initiatives that were undertaken, the civilian population, number one; and number two, control or, rather, the prevention of the breakthrough of the forces of the 28th Division; and taking care of the operational situation which would occur in the zones of the responsibility of the units who were on this axis of the breakthrough of the 28th Division. So they were three serious problems, and there truly was the necessity to balance out the responsibilities, to share them out if the Chief of Staff was available, as well as the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me take your expression, the expression that you use, in order to establish a balance. Would it not be better to have General Zivanovic, the Corps Commander in Zepa, and General Mladic, who is the chief of the Main Staff of the army, and the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps for the rest? Wouldn't that be a better solution?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is -- that would be the subject of expert analysis. I do not think so, no. I think that this was the most productive and best way, and now let's see why. First, General Zivanovic was the commander of the Drina Corps from earlier on, from before. General Zivanovic, as far as I know, was born in that area, in the zone of responsibility. I think the village's name was Ratkovici. That was his native village precisely in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, and if there was anybody who knew the problems of that area and that microregion, it was General Zivanovic. Furthermore, General Zivanovic was commander from before, as I said, and he was very well acquainted with what the corps could expect in tackling these two tasks, the forthcoming tasks. Therefore, there was no need, on the contrary, to replace the responsibility -- transfer these two competencies for the Zepa and that this be taken over by the Chief of Staff. I think that that would have been -- that that was a poorer solution, but probably the commander of the Main Staff was guided by that kind of logic. And another thing, President: It is not natural for the commander of all the forces to be appointed at a given period of time to be the commander of only a portion of the forces, a part of the troops. He is always commander of the main bulk of the troops, and the main bulk of the Drina Corps troops were still on the defensive positions and in defensive action, and the bulk of the corps remained outside the engagement of the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Mr. Visnjic, please continue. I think that Judge Riad has a question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: General Radinovic, you mentioned that General Krstic was appointed commander of the Drina Corps by the decree of the president as of July 15th, and you said that, of course, he could not take over his responsibilities until an operative post could create the conditions for him to take over duties. That was almost what you said. During this period, who was really concretely on the ground, active and responsible for the Drina Corps? The commander was not there. Who was really -- who could really handle the whole situation during that period? Did they refer to the commander in Zepa and ask him his opinion, or was there somebody completely -- was it Zivanovic, or did Zivanovic disappear from the picture from the moment he was appointed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to your question, Your Honour, Judge Riad, I can answer only on the basis of the available facts and information. As far as I know, General Zivanovic was in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, and he did not, by any act of command, was relieved of that function [as interpreted], those duties. Right up until the takeover of duty by General Krstic, he was the nominal and, for me, the de facto commander of the Corps, as there was no -- there is no information that he was prevented from commanding or was absent from the zone of responsibility at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And before the 15th, was General Krstic more or less the factual commander? It was known already that he was the commander. Did he really take matters in hand before he went to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th, in the evening, at a meeting at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters, after the taking over of Srebrenica - this was a meeting that was organised and presided over by the commander of the Main Staff - he received the assignment of preparing, organising, and executing the operation at Zepa. And from that moment on, he nominally and factually was commander of the operative group for Zepa, which implied a whole series of duties and responsibilities with shifting the forward command post from Pribicevac to Krivace, which meant that the operation had to be planned, which in turn meant that orders for the operation had to be compiled and drafted, as well as the plan of activities, which means the working cards and all the other plans prescribed for an operation of that kind. This requires the organisation of forces. It requires that the troops be brought in. It implies completely -- a completely secure zone in which those forces were to regroup, and it implies the deployment of troops to their initial positions, additional reconnoitring, translating the decision to the terrain and adapting it to the terrain, listening to the technical problems and other problems that the commanders of units were facing who were to take part in the Zepa operation, and reactions to all their requirements and demands, which in turn implies a complete monitoring of the situation and reactions to the problems which occur in the case of the operation and things that had to be corrected as things were moving on. Let me wind up my answer by saying that this was such a complex task, which required so many responsibilities, that General Krstic could not mentally or physically have the possibility of dealing with any other problems whatsoever except problems related to the proper planning and preparation and leadership of the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When did General Krstic have to leave for Zepa? What date exactly, if you know.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. General Krstic had to leave for Zepa before the beginning of the operation, and the operation started on the 14th, in the morning, from the command post -- it was the 13th, and General Krstic, if he wanted to be a professional soldier and to the level of his -- up to the level of his assignment, then he would have to have been in Zepa on several occasions before the operation was unleashed, first of all, to go for the first time with his operational officer, his intelligence officer, his chief of communications, his lead -- staff leader, officer, and to tell them what their duties were to prepare and install the forward command post for that operation. After that -- furthermore, General Krstic had to tour the units and commanders who were to be engaged in that operation. That was his second task, second duty. And during that time, he issued assignments to his assistant for operational affairs - and he was now the Chief of Staff of that operative group - to prepare documents for planning that operation. So that -- and he also had to appear at the command post at Vlasenica to see, with the deputy commanders -- to see to some affairs with them, which would allow the proper implementation of the operation. Then he would have to go back and see what had been done, whether the things assigned had actually been done. So he had to have intensive communication from the forward command post via the units to be included, up to the system of command for the Drina Corps, so as to prepare the operation as best as possible, and that means that his whole time would be taken up with all these activities. And if I were in his place, I could do nothing else apart from the Zepa operation. That would be my sole concern. I would have no time for anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: This is from the practical side only or even from the - what can I say? - official side? Because if I understood rightly, even before the operation was unleashed, General Krstic was completely excluded from any responsibilities other than the Drina Corps. Is that what you, in short, you want to say?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say that from the 11th, in the evening, when he was told of the decision, when the decision was made known to him that he was appointed commander of the operative group for the Zepa operation, he was nominally excluded from all his other responsibilities, and de facto he excluded himself because he didn't have time to do anything but -- to see to anything else but the Zepa operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it was a de facto necessity, but not an official -- his official responsibility stayed -- still remained till the operation started? As you said, if you were in his place, you would have had no time to do anything, but officially he was -- the operation -- till the operation started, he was officially responsible for his duties for the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The operation did not start at the very moment of its instigation, but its planning, preparation, and deployment of units, all that, as well as the preparation of the system of command and the command post. So that implies the time before the 14th. From the 11th to the 14th was the period of preparation and organisation for the operation, and from the 14th onwards was when the operation became implemented and he was physically -- he physically had to be there. But up until the 14th, he had to go to Zepa several times, but he had to be with his subordinate units as well, those units that he was to take to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'd just like to clarify the last one. You said on the 11th it was decided that would you go -- that would handle the Zepa operation. Was there a specific order that, from that moment, he had nothing else to do and that he was completely excluded from the other duties from that moment? Was there any specific order, or it was just, again, the practical impossibilities?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is the doctrinary principle in the system of command which need not be written down, written in writing. It is something that is a rule that holds true, that is applied. Had the commander of the Main Staff wanted not to change anything in the system of command, then he would -- to the commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic, he would have ordered him to implement the Zepa operation. That would have been his right. And General Zivanovic would then be duty-bound to organise the system of command as he saw fit, and then we would -- and we would see what kind of system he would have applied, and then we could have discussed that had that been the case. But the commander of the Main Staff considered that the solution and decision to appoint Krstic as commander of the operative group was the most productive and best solution. And as of that time when this was told to him, when Krstic was informed of this, Krstic was nominally excluded from the function of deputy corps commander and was authorised and duty-bound - and that is important, duty-bound - to organise and plan the Zepa operation and implement it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I think that what you wanted to put right on the LiveNote has disappeared from our screens, but I see you've made a note of it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but I can still see it on page 61, line 9. General Krstic is nominally excluded from the duty of Chief of Staff, and not "deputy of the corps commander" as it says in the transcript. I think he said the duty of Chief of Staff. That would be my first -- but it doesn't matter. Even if it said deputy, it doesn't matter; it's the same function. It's the same individual performing the two functions. The next correction that I have to make, once again for purposes of the record, relates to page 59, line 4, and the witness spoke about the fact that General Krstic came to the command to talk to the assistant commanders for certain departments at the command in Vlasenica; the "assistant commanders" of certain departments and not the "deputy commanders" as was written in the transcript. So that is my correction; not deputy commanders but assistant commanders. And I've just been told that on page 58, in line 1, the word was "tactical," and in the LiveNote it says "technical." The General said "tactical," not "technical."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, technical, tactical, it can be the same thing. Anyway, it's "tactical," not "technical." We put that right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, which system of command and control were applied in the Drina Corps from -- until the completion of Stupcanica, so July 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very few. This is a very rare zone of responsibility in which at the same time in a border area, relatively speaking, there were several structures or systems of command and control, and I'm quite sure of this, that the very existence of these several systems led to mutual disturbances and also for certain discrepancies in the system of command and control, the command system of the Drina Corps; also, certain elements of the command system of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska; thirdly, some elements of the control system of the government of Republika Srpska; then also a part of the leadership system within Republika Srpska; and finally, and this is very important for this testimony, also a certain level of independence of the security system of management and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let's start in some kind of order. The first system that you mentioned, the command system, that is, the command system of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, who was in command? Who issued orders for the engagement of the units of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska which in July of 1995 were in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders to the units of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska which were in this period in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps were issued by the Main Staff of the VRS, so elements -- by elements of its command system. I reach this conclusion based on the fact that I did not, during my research for this testimony, come up against even one document which the Main Staff would -- in which the Main Staff would authorise the command system of the Drina Corps to issue tasks to those units, to set tasks to those units, and to monitor their conduct and their activities. If there is no such document, if it doesn't exist, then for me, that means that the Main Staff did not wish to give the command authority to its directly-subordinated units to give to anybody else, other than its own command system.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In your research, what have you found out about the units -- which units of the Main Staff were in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, and which would be important for this testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of importance in this testimony, there are two units, and they are a battalion of the 65th Protective Motorised Regiment, and also the 10th Diversionary Detachment, which did not have its -- which was not based in the zone of responsibility but came to the zone of responsibility at a certain point, and, according to some testimony, this was on the 10th. All that I know is, on the video footage while the VRS was entering Srebrenica, I recognised the commander of that detachment, and, for me, this is information which is indicative of the fact that he appeared in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps on the 11th when I saw him in Srebrenica on that video footage. And of course, I watched that in order to prepare for this testimony. There are also testimonies which say that that detachment appeared there on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The 65th Protective Motorised Regiment also has one battalion which appears in the operation zone of Stupcanica 95 in the area of Zepa, and this is not the battalion you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is a police battalion of the 65th Protective Regiment, and this mechanised infantry battalion was in Zepa. It's a combat unit which was permanently engaged in Zepa. This is a battalion of the 65th regiment, and it's a police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, I just want to ask a similar question. An infantry battalion of the 65th regiment appears in the zone of responsibility -- excuse me, in the zone of actions of the Stupcanica 95 operation, and this is in the Zepa zone, isn't it? Is this true?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. To avoid confusion, we're talking about motorised formations. The difference between infantry and motorised in our terminology and doctrine is as follows: Infantry goes exclusively by foot, and these other ones can move using other means, but this difference is not really crucial.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, are there any documents from the Main Staff Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which oblige the command of the Drina Corps to cooperation with the forces of the Main Staff, and what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't come across any documents which would oblige the command of the Drina Corps to act together with the 10th Diversionary Regiment and the 10th [as interpreted] Protection Unit. I didn't come across such documents. None were presented to me, and I personally didn't come across any such documents. And what is most important for me, in the combat documents and command documents of the Drina Corps, there is no trace about this, about the fact that their superior command, the Main Staff had obliged them to establish relations of cooperation with such units of common action. So in this regard, I can conclude that the command of the Drina Corps was not authorised to act in this, in this manner; and for this, it would be essential that the Main Staff, with their order, would oblige them to enter into this type of relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I just want to ask a short question also because of the transcript. Is there any other document which would oblige the command of the Drina Corps to act together with the 10th Diversionary Detachment and the police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no such document. Such a document does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, in your view, which command system had the command responsibility for the conduct and the activities of the 10th Diversionary Detachment and the 65th Protection Regiment, its police battalion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command responsibility for the activities and the conduct of these units was borne by their superior command, and that is the Main Staff, i.e., those elements of the Main Staff which were superior to these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: These units, nevertheless, conducted tasks in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps. Does this mean that automatically the responsibility is transferred to the command system because of their activities? Does this mean that this would be conveyed automatically, transferred automatically to the command system of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would not, for the simple reason that the zone of the Drina Corps is also a zone of responsibility of the VRS, and for all units of the Main Staff which it did not directly, explicitly, or by its act of command did not subordinate to the command of the Drina Corps or order it to act in cooperation with those units. So practically, the Drina Corps and the command of the Drina Corps was in this way completely excluded from any kind of command competence and, therefore, command responsibility. I also want to add: If, in the command system and the system of informing, the command of the Drina Corps found out that these units committed something that was proscribed under regulations, then they would be obliged, the Drina Corps, and the command system would be obliged to act in accordance or exactly the same way that any officer or any member of an army would behave when they found out that somebody was acting against rules and regulations, meaning that procedures would have to be initiated and investigations which would be required in such a particular case. So only in this regard can there be responsibility for the conduct of others in their zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to give the witness Prosecution Exhibit 649.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, you have Prosecution Exhibit 649 in front of you. You are already familiar with this document. You came across it in your research. So I would like you to comment on the command responsibility of the Drina Corps in this context, for the activities cited in this document.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two things are important here. First, the commander of the Main Staff orders a group of three officers from the Main Staff, Colonels Trkulja, Stankovic, and Sladojevic, to go to the command of the 1st Zvornik Brigade in order to assist in the joining of the forces for the coordination of combat operation, and as we know from my today testimony, the situation in their zone of responsibility was very difficult. This was on the 17th of July, 1995. It's important to note here that the Main Staff is sending this group of officers to review the situation, and, together with the commander of the brigade, to consider the situation, and, together with the commander, draw up a plan in order to resolve the situation. So in this first part, in points 1 and 2, the commander of the Main Staff does not rule out the commander of the Zvornik Brigade from the command system, nor from the -- from command responsibility for his zone. He is just sending him help. This is one form of interference, or a mixing of the Main Staff command system with the command system of the Drina Corps, but it's absolutely legitimate. So the intent -- with the intent to help, because this was the most sensitive point in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps. In paragraph 3, the commander of the Main Staff orders that the territory is combed in zone of -- which he has indicated. So this is within the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, with the aim of discovering and destroying lagging Muslim groups. And to command all the mentioned forces in the execution of that task, he appoints staff officer for military police from the security administration of the Main Staff of the VRS, Colonel Keserovic, and the officers -- or the forces that he places at his disposal for that task are the 1st Bratunac Brigade, the 1st Milici Brigade, 67th Communications Regiment, a battalion of the military police of the 65th Protection Regiment, and forces of the MUP engaged in the wider areas of Bratunac, Milici, Drinjaca. So all of these forces are placed under the command of Colonel Keserovic, the officer from the Main Staff, and authorises him to command those forces in the period from the 17th, when this order was issued, until the 19th of July, and with those activities and, conditionally speaking, this operation, to conduct this operation from the command post of the police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. And this regiment, as we know, was in Nova Kasaba. So the Main Staff is installing a command post which would unify all of the forces which would comb the territory in that zone. And practically, not only do they include those forces which are directly subordinated to the Main Staff in the first degree of subordination, but also units of the Drina Corps, i.e., its two brigades, the Milici and the Bratunac Brigades. I personally think that in this way it can best be seen how in a small area there are several command instances which must also have some kind of interference effect. So not only do they help each other, but they also interfere with each other as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That document is not from this case. It's a mistake. So the registrar will probably remove that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm a soldier. Nothing can surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Shall we move to the next question. In the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, there is also a special brigade, a special MUP brigade. Which unit is that? In the command sense, who is it subordinated to? So as not to enter into too many details, what is the doctrinary principle regarding the engagement of police forces in the zone of engagement of military forces? So could you please tell us a little bit about that.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me whenever I respond to your questions not to use -- not to have in mind the type of categories that we have in my profession, in the military profession, so I think that most of the interpretation problems occur because of that fact, and I do apologise for that. The doctrinary principle which is applicable: Whenever police units find themselves in the area of responsibility of military forces during combat activities, the unity of action is ensured by the most senior officer in whose area of responsibility these activities are taking place. We're faced here with a rather serious and complex problem of interpretation of this doctrinary principle and with the application of this principle to the case in point. The operation Krivaja 95 is completed. It came to an end on the 11th of July. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the operation was completed on the 11th of July. Thereby, the Drina Corps commander no longer had the obligation to act as a unifying factor of the police forces in his area of responsibility, because Krivaja 95 had come to an end. There was no operation Krivaja 95. The police forces appeared in the area of responsibility of the corps after the completion of the Krivaja 95 operation. In view of the fact that the special detachment of the MUP appeared in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps after the completion of the operation, for any type of command relationship between the Drina Corps command and the brigade in question, there must have been -- there should have been a relevant document, a relevant act of command which would go in both directions. First of all, the brigade in question is subordinated to the Ministry of the Interior of the government of Republika Srpska. For that brigade, that is to say, for this particular detachment of this brigade to be engaged in any sense outside that area and outside the scope of the assignments given to it by the Ministry of the Interior - and I am not familiar with those assignments; that doesn't fall within my expertise - there has to be a specific mention in an act of command issued by the ministry for what kind of assignments and for what period of time that particular detachment is being seconded. For the Drina Corps commander to have the mandate to use such a unit, there has to be a specific mention in the act of command issued by the Main Staff as to the time framework for the use of this particular unit, and also a mention of the type of assignment this unit is going to be used. During my research, during my preparation for this testimony, I haven't come across a single such document, and therefore my conclusion is that the brigade was under command of its command system, i.e., the Ministry of the Interior, or some organ from the top leadership of the state, which remains unknown to me because I do not dispose of any analytical data or information for any such conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, do you think we can have a break at this point? Would this be convenient for you? Fifteen-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can ask the usher to prepare for us OTP Exhibit 404, footnote 70, and one more Prosecution exhibit, number 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, let us now address the issue of the third command system in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're both in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You can use mine, my English version. [Interpretation] If we can have the English version on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, you should have the B/C/S version in front of you. General Radinovic, in your research, did you find the document on the appointment of the civilian commissioner for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The answer to your question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell the Chamber briefly what was the procedure of establishing civilian authority in the territory of the Srebrenica municipality and their relationship with the command structure, command system of the Drina Corps, possible distribution of authorities; and generally speaking, could you tell us your conclusions about that issue?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will strictly abide by this document in my response. The document was issued on the 11th of July by the president of Republika Srpska, 11th of July, 1995. It is a decision on the appointment of the civilian commissioner for the Serbian municipality of Srebrenica. The president of Republika Srpska appointed Miroslav Deronjic to the post of the civilian commissioner, and he gave him the following obligations and duties, in agreement with the president of Republika Srpska and the government of Republika Srpska, to establish the functions of the municipal authority organs and to ensure conditions for their efficient functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, sorry, excuse me. It's just a correction on the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It was just a correction on the exhibit number, Mr. Visnjic. I think it may have been a lapse, a slip of the tongue, but it's 404, 90, this document. It says 70 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Cayley. Indeed, this is the Exhibit 404, footnote 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So the first duty of the civilian commissioner was to establish and ensure the efficient functioning of civilian authority. The president of Republika Srpska thereby gave him a very high level of responsibility. He obliges him to do that in cooperation with the president and the government of Republika Srpska, so that is a very high level, indeed. He is not transmitting that authority to the regional level, but he, as the president, is keeping that authority for himself. Second obligation that he is interested with is to cooperate with the Ministry of the Interior with a view of establishing a public security station there. Thirdly, he is obliged to ensure that the civilian and military organs in respect of all citizens -- so he is to ensure that all civilian and military organs treat all citizens who participated in combat against the army of Republika Srpska as prisoners of war, and to ensure that the civilian population can freely choose where they will live or move to. This is a very serious duty indeed with which the civilian commissioner is entrusted on the 11th of July, 1995, on the same day when this huge humanitarian problem arose, that is, the grouping of the civilian population in Potocari and around the base in Potocari, that is, as of the moment when they were actually faced with this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, what was the highest level authority signed by this commissioner?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I should like to have Prosecution document number 47.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, let me say that the highest governing document that was signed by this commissioner was the statement of the representative of the civilian authority on the evacuation of the civilian population from the Srebrenica enclave. So that document was signed by Miroslav Deronjic, representative of the civilian authority of the Srebrenica enclave, Nesib Mandzic, and an UNPROFOR representative, obviously, a member of the Dutch Battalion who was there to ensure the protection of the safe area. In this document, we read that the evacuation of the civilian population from the Srebrenica enclave has been carried out as regards the Serb side in a correct and fair manner, and that the agreement of the evacuation was fully honoured and respected, that the evacuation was carried out properly. During the evacuation, there were no incidents on either side, and the Serb side respected all of the regulations contained in the Geneva Conventions and the international laws of war. It is true that, after the comma here, we can read the following sentence: "As regards the convoys that were escorted by the United Nation Forces." I'm sorry, we did not see the original on the transcript. If I may, I should like to give you my comment of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, the Chamber has already heard the reasons and the way in which this sentence was added to the text, but if you wish to comment on it, you may do so briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't intend to discuss the reasons why the sentence was added, but I must say that it is an important indication for me, as an expert, who approached this matter in the most professional way. It is indicative of two things: First of all, that the procedure of the moving out of the population from the area contained certain elements which were not allowed. There were elements of improper, prohibited behaviour. Second, that those who were involved, or rather who were in charge to ensure that, to ensure that respect and protection throughout the procedure, failed to do that, including the representative of the UNPROFOR command. The obligation in question is fairly simple, and one needs not be an expert in order to understand and see in what way such a procedure could be carried out in a proper and safe manner. I'm not trying to place the blame on anyone here or to weigh the blame of the parties involved in any way. I just want to note the fact that the mechanism of the United Nations, who was in place in Potocari and Srebrenica in the relevant times, was duty-bound to see to it that the procedure is properly controlled in order to prevent what was actually -- what happened. What was the reason why this sentence was added, I don't know; however, it is beyond dispute that at this moment we would be much closer to the truth had that been done, and they indeed -- he indeed had enough resources to carry that out, to fulfil that obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, in your research, did you notice a relatively independent commanding line that would go vertically in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that that vertical line was indeed established in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps and that that line of command exerted a certain influence and affected the effectiveness of the control over the situation in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. Your previous answer, does it refer to a relatively independent command line of security organs in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I ask the usher to prepare for us OTP Exhibit D402 [as interpreted], footnote 10, and Exhibit -- Defence Exhibit D158.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, the first exhibit, 402, should be preceded with a "P." It is a Prosecution Exhibit, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we need page 33, General, the Serbo-Croatian version. It's on page 32. Very well. Page 32, then, General. Could the usher find the relevant page, please, in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... same page. It's page 30 in English. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, this document regulates the activities of the security organs. Can you tell the Trial Chamber briefly what your comments are, the portion of the document which you consider to be important.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the rules on competencies, we see that the obligations of the security organs are properly prescribed in the corps command, that is to say, the assistant commander for security. I do not have any special comments to make, but I'd just like to draw your attention to paragraph 9, paragraph 9, which, in the normative sense -- as I say, in the normative sense, this paragraph gives the framework under which it would be possible for that service to become independent, and I quote: "Expert directing security organs," as written, "and the military police in the corps command and units and in other --" It says JNA units here, "in the zone of responsibility." Up until then, I don't contest anything, but now we come to the part of the sentence that can be contested: "... organising, directing, and coordinating their activities," that is to say, coordinating their activities, "providing assistance and controlling their work," and I underline this phrase, "controlling their work." So in paragraph 9, that is what is stipulated. There are certain normative points for the independence of those organs. There is a basis for that in paragraph 9. Unfortunately, there are far more practical experiences which testify to the fact and show that that system, command system, very frequently, from the functional turns into the command system. And believe me when I say that I personally, in the course of my professional career, I have had occasion to experience something of that system, but of course, that needn't hold true for this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we're talking about normative regulation, I should like to ask the usher to place on the ELMO Defence Exhibit D158. It is an excerpt from the regulations of the Security Service which the Prosecution submitted to this Tribunal, and it has been registered as the -- as a Prosecution exhibit, as Prosecution Exhibit 402, footnote 34.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: This is just an excerpt indicating paragraph 29 [as interpreted] of those regulations. Could I have your comments on paragraph 49?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Forty-nine, not twenty-nine, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 49, particularly the second paragraph of 49, offers even broader scope in the normative sense for that functional system to be transformed into a command system. And let me quote, let me read it and see what it's all about, and I quote. The data and information which represents a secret, which is confidential, the officers from point 1, which is the security organ, may pass on information to other authorised security organ officers or other persons only with the authorisation of his superior officer in the security organ. So I should like to underline that in particular. So the information which the security organ considers to be secret and confidential, he can inform only persons who are authorised about this pursuant to a decision of his superior in the security organ. And now we have this duality in the system of command. All the assistants to the commander are subordinated to the commander, and that is incontestable. It is incontestable, namely, that the Corps Commander must have command responsibility over all portions of his command, including the security organ or his assistant for security. But this point of article 49 in the normative sense authorises the security organ in the corps command to make his own assessment as to what is an official secret, and he need not inform anybody of that if the superior security organ does not agree. In concrete terms, this would mean if the assistant for security of the commander of the Drina Corps were to consider something to be an official secret, then he, that is, including his -- he can inform his commander of that and other persons, he can do so only with permission from the assistant for security of the Main Staff. And that is how we have a crack in the norms, in the normative acts; and this fissure, this crack, exists in the system of command which leads to this vertical parallel command which can be opposed to the legally accepted doctrinary system of command for the corps command. And in this system, you have the functioning, vertically speaking, of the security organs from the Main Staff via the Drina Corps down to the brigades, including the military police, and the possibilities are that this will impede the system of command and interfere with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, by virtue of his function in the system of command, whose duty would it be to deal with POWs, prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the system of command of the prisoners of war by nature of this duty, it would have to be the security organs and intelligence organs who would deal with this, but first and foremost the security organs. And this is based on normative documents and on doctrinary documents. It is provided for there. If the problem of prisoners of war is a security problem, which it is, then it is an intelligence problem as well because the interviewing of prisoners of war can give us intelligence data and information as to the situation and position of the enemy, his intentions, and so on and so forth. So they are a security problem primarily, and it is a problem which, in principle, in the sense of control, in the sense of processing, examination, interrogation, selection, perhaps finding elements of crime amongst this population of prisoners of war, that is customarily the duty of the security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: How was the relationship regulated towards the prisoners of war within the command of the VRS, starting from the Supreme Commander of the VRS via the Main Staff down to the command of the Drina Corps? Was there a systematic chain and normative documents in that respect?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, attitude towards humanitarian law and prisoners of war, that relationship in the army of Republika Srpska is prescribed in the same way as it is in the Yugoslav People's Army. When the conflict broke out in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and I am unfortunately an eyewitness to that and a living one, then the Yugoslav People's Army organised seminars under the leadership of the head of the legal department, and unleashed a whole mechanism of lawyers and legal experts in our army who compiled manuals and textbooks, prescribing how units and the forces generally are duty-bound to adhere to the international laws and international conventions and conduct towards prisoners of war. According to that same principle, in the army of Republika Srpska, steps were taken of that kind. The president of the Republic and the Supreme Commander in his own acts made it incumbent upon all the levels of command in the VRS to have proper conduct towards the prisoners of war, in keeping with the provisions of international humanitarian law. That was binding. It was a binding document for all members of the army of Republika Srpska. And it is in keeping with that document that he ordered the corresponding ministry to draft the relevant documents, manuals, textbooks, and it included the obligation of the command system of the army, so that all members of the army should become acquainted with that, those documents, and should adhere to the principles prescribed therein. In keeping with that obligation, all constitutive acts of command, all orders issued by the commanders contained a provision with respect to the way in which the forces were to treat the prisoners of war, and this treatment was in conformity with international humanitarian law and the conventions, and that is what the order for Krivaja 95 of the Drina Corps Commander also contained.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask the usher to provide the witness with Defence Exhibit D156, D157, and to prepare Prosecution Exhibits 428 and 532 [Realtime transcript read in error "532"]. So we first have Defence Exhibit 157. I see in the exhibit [as interpreted] that it says Prosecution Exhibits 428 and "532."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, this is Defence Exhibit 157. It is a document issued by the command of the Drina Corps. It is number 2-160, dated the 18th of December, 1992. It is signed by Colonel Prstojevic. My question is a very simple one: Is this document the type of document with which the commands informed their officers of with respect to the need to adhere to international norms in war?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an act, a document issued by the Drina Corps, as we see, on the 18th of December, 1992 - that means more than a month after it was established - and this was an urgent information about the need for complying to international norms in war. And it explicitly states the duty of men to adhere to that, and the first sentence states how this is to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask the usher to place on the ELMO Defence Exhibit D156.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, you have before you a similar document. It is dated the 15th of July, 1993. The number of the document is written in hand in the right-hand corner. It is number 678. The document is signed by Colonel Milutin Skocajic. Is this document too an example of the type of document by which officers are cautioned, that is to say, members of the VRS and Drina Corps, are cautioned of the need to adhere to the principles of the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And of course the regulations of international warfare.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it is entitled "Behaviour Towards War Prisoners" and it is written in that spirit. I don't think I need read it because, from the word go, it is binding and mandatory, in keeping with the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask the usher to show the witness the following exhibit. It is Exhibit 428, page 4 and 5 in the Serbian version, section regarding security. This is item 10B.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows, General Radinovic: You mentioned a little while ago that, in the order for active combat activities, Krivaja 95, as part of the functional system that was entrusted with it in the functional system, so in that part there is also a procedure regarding the treatment of possible prisoners of war. Is this document in keeping with the previous documents and the rules of international law regarding this question?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The commander of the corps in active combat," and we're talking about item 10B, "the security are ordered by the organs of security, the military police. They will indicate the areas for gathering and securing the prisoners of war and war booty. In dealing with prisoners of war and the civilian population, behave in every way in accordance with the Geneva Conventions." So this is an obligation that arises from everything that was stated in the VRS regarding treatment of prisoners of war and civilians, and this was ordered from the top of the state, from state authorities, and it goes down to units, both tactical and operative units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to ask the usher to place Prosecution Exhibit 532 on the ELMO. It's a document from the 13th of July, 1995, and this exhibit is the same as Defence Exhibit D81.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, this is a document of the Main Staff. Could you please comment on the part of this document that specially concerns paragraph 3, item 3, regarding the functioning and the treatment of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the document of the Main Staff of the VRS, sent to all the units of the Drina Corps, including its brigades and the commander, there is an explicit order, which states, under item 3: "Place captured and disarmed Muslims in suitable premises where they can be guarded by small forces and report immediately to the Superior Command." This is very clear and precise, and it's an order about what to do with prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, the document was issued by the Main VRS Staff. In your view, what would be the chain of custody of prisoners of war to the Superior Command? Let's assume that one group of prisoners were captured by members of a unit of the Bratunac Brigade, for example.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document obliges the battalion to inform the brigade command about the capture, and it's up to the command how it will regulate things further. The command brigade is obligated to inform the command of the corps, and the corps command should inform the Main Staff. Treatment of prisoners of war is not in the competence of any level of the army of the VRS but in the competence of the Main Staff, i.e., the Supreme Command, because they have exchange commissions and that is their obligation, and that is why this Main Staff order states that the treatment of prisoners of war should be in coordination with the vertical command structure, from the lowest tactical units all the way up to the top of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Radinovic, this order was issued on the 13th of July, 1995. In the course of your research, did you find out which units on the 13th of July were deployed along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road and also the road from Konjevic Polje to Milici?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I learned, the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road, a special detachment of the MUP brigade was deployed there. And then on the road to Konjevic Polje, Nova Kasaba, there was the police battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I still have a half an hour or a little less, so I would like to suggest, if you agree, that we stop the hearing today, and I will try tomorrow morning to be as brief as possible and to maybe take up less than half an hour in order to complete my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you, Mr. Visnjic, and I hope that you will be able to work out your plan from now until tomorrow morning in order for you to be able to finish. Yes, Mr. Visnjic. I think that we will then finish this examination-in-chief tomorrow morning, but that means that the Prosecutor will also start the cross-examination tomorrow morning. I don't know whether you are able to tell us, but do you have any idea, Mr. Cayley, as to the time you think you will need for the cross-examination? I know I have already asked you the question, and I know that you are fully prepared to provide me with an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm well aware you want me to get through this as vigorously and as rapidly as possible, and I am organising myself so to do. I do not believe I will be finished by Friday, but I do believe that I will be able to finish by Monday. It will be three days or less, not three days or more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there is one thing that we should adopt as principle, and that we should stick to it: You must not exceed the time of the examination-in-chief; otherwise, we will be turning things upside down, as you know that there is a certain logic in the presentation of evidence in the conduct of the Defence case and the Prosecution case. You will be given enough time, but please bear in mind that you should not exceed the time of the examination-in-chief. If necessary, the registrar can tell us exactly how much time the Defence used for the examination-in-chief, but I hope that won't be necessary and that we can trust you. Mr. Visnjic will finish early tomorrow morning, and you will start your cross-examination. So we will convene tomorrow morning at 9:20 as usual.
